<comment datatype="string">L-lyxose is an uncommon sugar in nature, and wild-type <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> can not utilize it as a sole source of carbon
and energy.  However, mutations can arise that allow <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> to metabolize L-lyxose through the use of
enzymes of the rhamnose, arabinose and 2,3-diketo-L-gulonate systems. 
<p>
L-lyxose enters the cell through the <I>rhaT</I>-encoded rhamnose transporter.  It is then isomerized to
L-xylulose by <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=RHAMNISOM-MONOMER">L-rhamnose isomerase</a>. 
<p>
Two types of mutations then allow further utilization of L-xylulose.  Not shown here, a mutated from of
<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=RHAMNULOKIN-MONOMER">rhamnulokinase</a> can phosphorylate L-xylulose, yielding L-xylulose-1-phosphate.  Further
metabolism to dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glycolate occurs through the
<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=RHAMNULPALDOL-MONOMER">rhamnulose-1-phosphate aldolase</a> and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=LACTALDDEHYDROG-MONOMER">aldehyde dehydrogenase A, NAD-linked</a> enzymes.  These products can enter glycolate
degradation and glycolysis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1650346">Badia91</a>].  
<p>
As shown here, L-xylulose can be phosphorylated by <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=LYXK-MONOMER">L-xylulose kinase</a> in a mutant in which YiaJ, the repressor
for the <I>yiaKLMNO-lyxK-sgbHUE</I> operon, has been disrupted [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7961955">Sanchez94</a>].  L-xylulose-5-phosphate is
then further metabolized by <a href="http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/new-image?object=EG12286-MONOMER">putative L-xylulose 5-phosphate 3-epimerase</a> (so far only a predicted function) and either of two
L-ribulose 5-phosphate 4-epimerases (SgbE or AraD) to D-xylulose-5-phosphate, which then enters the
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=NONOXIPENT-PWY">pentose phosphate pathway (non-oxidative branch) I</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9525947">Badia98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10913097">Ibanez00</a>].
<p>
The enzymes of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=RHAMCAT-PWY">L-rhamnose degradation I</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=ARABCAT-PWY">L-arabinose degradation I</a> are inducible by L-lyxose as well
[<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1650346">Badia91</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10913097">Ibanez00</a>].
<p>
Review: Mayer, C. and W. Boos, Hexose/Pentose and Hexitol/Pentitol Metabolism, EcoSal Module 3.4.1 [<a href="http://www.ecosal.org/">EcoSal</a>]</comment>

observed: In the metabolic system under study here, a 3-epimerase activity could convert the l-xylulose-5-phosphate generated by l-xylulose kinase into the l-ribulose-5-phosphate substrate of YiaS (Fig. 2). However, all attempts to obtain experimental evidence of the 3-epimerase activity have been unsuccessful so far. This included the purification of YiaR through its fusion to the protein glutathione S-transferase and separation of the fused protein by affinity chromatography with glutathione to assay the enzymatic activity. The studies performed on YiaR did not rule out its possible role as a 3-epimerase and suggested either a low stability of YiaR or the lack of a key cofactor required for activity and/or stability.

Either the assay conditions we used for UlaE are inappropriate for SgbU or the sgbU gene contains a mutation that renders its encoded protein inactive, thereby preventing utilization of l-dehydroascorbate.

observed: The induction of the ara system by l-lyxose and the high similarity displayed by YiaS and AraD suggest that AraD could complement the YiaS function in strain JA196. To determine whether AraD complemented YiaS function, the araD mutation of strain MC4100 was transferred into the genetic background of strain JA196 (yiaS::cat) by the following strategy. (i) A Tn10 marker was transduced from strain CAG12095 (13) into strain MC4100, and tetracycline-resistant transductants that retained the inability to utilize l-arabinose were selected. (ii) One of these transductants (strain JA197) was subsequently used to transduce the two linked markers into strain JA196. A double mutant (strain JA198) was isolated and transformed with plasmids containing yiaS or araD and tested for its ability to utilize both l-lyxose and l-arabinose. None of the transformants analyzed displayed impairment in either of these metabolisms, showing that the 4-epimerase function could be supplied by either of the two YiaS and AraD proteins.

observed: The His-tagged proteins were purified with columns of chelating Sepharose Fast Flow (Pharmacia Biotech) charged with Ni2+. Cell lysates were applied to the column in binding buffer, washed with 15% elute buffer (1 M imidazole, 0.5 M NaCl, 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.9, and 5 mM MgCl2)-85% wash buffer (60 mM imidazole, 0.5 M NaCl, 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.9, and 5 mM MgCl2), and eluted with 50% binding buffer-50% strip buffer (100 mM EDTA, 0.5 mM NaCl, 20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.9, and 5 mM MgCl2). The N-terminal His tags (except for YiaK and LyxK) were removed with thrombin (Pharmacia Biotech) according to the manufacturer’s instructions, and the proteins were purified to homogeneity on a ResourceQ column (Pharmacia Biotech) equilibrated with binding buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.9, 5 mM MgCl2) and eluted with a linear gradient of 0 M to 0.5 M elution buffer (1 M NaCl, 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.9, 5 mM MgCl2). For YiaK, transformed cells were grown at 37°C in M9 minimal medium supplemented with 0.1 M glucose and ampicillin (100 μg/ml) to an OD600 of 0.6 and induced with 0.5 mM IPTG for 2 h; the protein was purified as described above.

A typical PCR mixture (100 μl) contained 1 ng of genomic DNA, 10 μl of 10× Pfx amplification buffer (Life Technologies), 1 mM MgSO4, 0.4 mM concentrations of each of the four deoxynucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs), 40 pmol of each primer (Table 1), and 5 U of Platinum Pfx DNA polymerase. The genes were amplified using a PTC-200 gradient thermal cycler (MJ Research), with the following parameters: 94°C for 2 min; followed by 40 cycles of 94°C for 1 min, a gradient annealing temperature range of 45 to 60°C for 1 min 15 s and 68°C for 2 min; and a final extension of 68°C for 10 min. The amplified genes were cloned into a modified pET15-b (Novagen) vector in which the N-terminal His tag contains 10 instead of the usual 6 His residues.

observed:
<comment datatype="string">L-ribulose 5-phosphate 4-epimerase catalyzes the third step in the pathway for degradation of L-arabinose, the epimerization at the C4 carbon to form D-xylulose-5-phosphate, which enters the <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=NONOXIPENT-PWY">pentose phosphate pathway (non-oxidative branch) I</a>.
<p>
The enzyme catalyzes epimerization via a carbon-carbon bond cleavage analogous to a class II aldolase reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9548961">Johnson98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10769138">Lee00</a>].  The H97N and other mutants can catalyze an aldolase reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9548961">Johnson98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10769139">Lee00a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732896">Samuel01</a>].  The binding site for Zn<sup>2+</sup>, the physiological metal cofactor, has been identified by sequence similarity and mutagenesis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10769139">Lee00a</a>] as well as in the crystal structure [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732895">Luo01</a>].  Mutagenesis of the predicted phosphate-binding pocket results in a significant increase in K<sub>m</sub>, and Asp120 was identified as one of two key catalytic acid/base residues [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732896">Samuel01</a>].
<p>
The enzyme was crystallized [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8520491">Andersson95</a>], and crystal structures of the wild type [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732895">Luo01</a>] and a mutant enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732896">Samuel01</a>] have been solved.  Consistent with its aldolase-type reaction mechanism, the structure shows close overall similarity to that of L-fuculose-1-phosphate aldolase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732895">Luo01</a>].
<p>

The enzyme was crystallized [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8520491">Andersson95</a>], and crystal structures of the wild type [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732895">Luo01</a>] and a mutant enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732896">Samuel01</a>] have been solved.  Consistent with its aldolase-type reaction mechanism, the structure shows close overall similarity to that of L-fuculose-1-phosphate aldolase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732895">Luo01</a>].
<p>
(Note: Several of the recent studies, including crystallization of the enzyme, appear to be using the enzyme from <i>E. coli</i> B/r UP1000 (gene originally cloned by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3549454">Lee86</a>]) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10769138">Lee00</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10769139">Lee00a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732895">Luo01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11732896">Samuel01</a>].)  Most studies of the enzyme and its genetics were done in <i>E. coli</i> B/r.  
<p>
Earlier studies of the enzyme from <i>E. coli</i> B/r described its purification [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4879898">Lee68</a>], its catalytic mechanism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4560420">Davis72</a>] and summarized its properties [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/236468">Gielow75</a>]. The nucleotide sequence of the coding region of <i>araD</i> from <i>E. coli</i> K-12 W3110 was shown to be 97% identical to that of <i>E. coli</i> B/r, and the deduced amino acid sequences showed 98.7% identity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2251150">Mineno90</a>].
<p>
AraD from <i>E. coli</i> DH1 (a K-12 derivative) forms a stable homotetramer as determined by size exclusion chromatography [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9548961">Johnson98</a>].
<p>
Metabolic engineering work in yeast has utilized <i>E. coli</i> <i>araD</i> and <i>araB</i>, and <i>Bacillus subtilis</i> or <i>B. licheniformis araA</i> in the fermentation of L-arabinose to ethanol [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12839792">Becker03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18263741">Wiedemann08</a>].
<p>
Transcription of the <i>araBAD</i> operon is induced in the presence of L-arabinose by the transcription factor AraC [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1093171">Casadaban75</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7768852">Johnson95</a>].  <i>araBAD</i> expression can also induced by L-lyxose [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10913097">Ibanez00</a>].
<p>
<i>araD</i> mutants can not utilize L-arabinose for growth [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13829634">Gross59</a>] and accumulate L-ribulose 5-phosphate when incubated with L-arabinose [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13890280">Englesberg62</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">L-lyxose is an uncommon sugar in nature, and wild-type <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> can not utilize it as a sole source of carbon
and energy.  However, mutations can arise that allow <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-562"><i>Escherichia coli</i></a> to metabolize L-lyxose through the use of
enzymes of the rhamnose, arabinose and 2,3-diketo-L-gulonate systems. 
<p>
L-lyxose enters the cell through the <I>rhaT</I>-encoded rhamnose transporter.  It is then isomerized to
L-xylulose by <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=RHAMNISOM-MONOMER">L-rhamnose isomerase</a>. 
<p>
Two types of mutations then allow further utilization of L-xylulose.  Not shown here, a mutated from of
<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=RHAMNULOKIN-MONOMER">rhamnulokinase</a> can phosphorylate L-xylulose, yielding L-xylulose-1-phosphate.  Further
metabolism to dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glycolate occurs through the
<a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=RHAMNULPALDOL-MONOMER">rhamnulose-1-phosphate aldolase</a> and <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=LACTALDDEHYDROG-MONOMER">aldehyde dehydrogenase A, NAD-linked</a> enzymes.  These products can enter glycolate
degradation and glycolysis [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1650346">Badia91</a>].  
<p>
As shown here, L-xylulose can be phosphorylated by <a href="/gene?orgid=META&id=LYXK-MONOMER">L-xylulose kinase</a> in a mutant in which YiaJ, the repressor
for the <I>yiaKLMNO-lyxK-sgbHUE</I> operon, has been disrupted [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7961955">Sanchez94</a>].  L-xylulose-5-phosphate is
then further metabolized by <a href="http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/new-image?object=EG12286-MONOMER">putative L-xylulose 5-phosphate 3-epimerase</a> (so far only a predicted function) and either of two
L-ribulose 5-phosphate 4-epimerases (SgbE or AraD) to D-xylulose-5-phosphate, which then enters the
<a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=NONOXIPENT-PWY">pentose phosphate pathway (non-oxidative branch) I</a> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9525947">Badia98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10913097">Ibanez00</a>].
<p>
The enzymes of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=RHAMCAT-PWY">L-rhamnose degradation I</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=ARABCAT-PWY">L-arabinose degradation I</a> are inducible by L-lyxose as well
[<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1650346">Badia91</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10913097">Ibanez00</a>].
<p>
Review: Mayer, C. and W. Boos, Hexose/Pentose and Hexitol/Pentitol Metabolism, EcoSal Module 3.4.1 [<a href="http://www.ecosal.org/">EcoSal</a>]</comment>

texts.value: Transcription factor involved in the utilization of L-ascorbate (PubMed:30137486, PubMed:31892694). Negatively controls the transcription of the yiaKLMNOPQRS (yiaK-S or yiaK-yiaL-yiaM-yiaN-yiaO-lyxK-sgbH-sgbU-sgbE) operon, which is involved in the L-ascorbate degradation pathway (PubMed:10913096, PubMed:30137486). It may repress the ascorbate utilization pathway, therefore regulating the level of D-xylulose-5-phosphate that feeds into the pentose phosphate pathway (PubMed:30137486). It is involved in the utilization of plant-derived materials as nutrients for survival, including ascorbate from fruits and galacturonate from plant pectin (PubMed:31892694). In addition, the targets include genes involved in the utilization of other plant-derived materials as nutrients such as fructose, sorbitol, glycerol and fructoselysine (PubMed:31892694). Acts by binding to specific DNA sequences (PlaR-box) in the promoter regions of target operons, repressing their transcription (PubMed:10913096, PubMed:31892694)

binding.version: Inspected complete primary article body; original PMC94634.html retrieved 2026-10-12

observed: Transcription of the yiaK-S genes as a single unit was also supported by the properties of lacZ fusions presented in Fig. 1. These operon fusions were transferred to strains ECL1 and JA134. Among these fusions, only the one corresponding to the leading yiaK displayed β-galactosidase activity under any of the growth conditions used, which included CAA in the presence or absence of l-lyxose. Expression of the (yiaK-lacZ) fusion in the genetic background of strain ECL1 resulted in a β-galactosidase activity of 42 Miller units, while its expression in the yiaJ mutant strain JA134 displayed high levels of β-galactosidase activity (4,250 Miller units) in both the absence and the presence of l-lyxose. These observations indicated that the only functional promoter for the structural genes is located upstream of yiaK.

evidence.source_assertion: Issuing MG1655 NCBI Gene identifies lyxK and its exact EcoCyc frame EG12284. This binds the native transcription target to the Entrez gene, not directly to enzyme catalytic activity.
Native REG0-4905 assigns + regulation of yiaKp1 (PM692) by CPLX0-226. This concerns transcription of the yiaK-S unit, not direct enzyme control; JA134 has the native PlaR lesion.

binding.version: Inspected complete primary article body; original PMC94634.html retrieved 2026-10-12

observed: Our results indicate that the yiaK-S operon is regulated by carbon sources. As shown, succinate increases and glucose reduces its expression in the absence of the repressor. This promoter strongly responds to glucose catabolite repression through the Crp site 1; in contrast, the yiaJ promoter, which overlaps with the yiaK-S promoter and is transcribed divergently from it, responds to the same conditions with increased expression. The mechanism for this yiaJ activation seems to be based on the nonoccupancy of Crp site 1 by the Crp-cAMP complex, hence releasing the obstruction to yiaJ transcription. In this way, catabolite repression of yiaK-S expression is coordinately helped by the increase in the repressor synthesis. In the absence of glucose, Crp-cAMP complex binds to Crp site 1 activating yiaK-S expression and obstructing the yiaJ-encoded repressor expression and synthesis. In spite of the binding observed to Crp site 2, its function remains unknown.

observed: To determine whether IHF influences yiaK-S expression in vivo, we examined the effect of a mutation in himA or in himD3. The himA::cat and the himD3::cat alleles were transferred from strain HN1491 and strain K2704 to a JA134 background by P1 transduction, yielding strains JA184 and JA185. Introduction of each of these IHF mutations produced a fourfold decrease in β-galactosidase activity in these mutant strains compared with that of the isogenic wild type (data not shown). These results suggest that IHF activates yiaK-S expression.

observed: To determine whether IHF influences yiaK-S expression in vivo, we examined the effect of a mutation in himA or in himD3. The himA::cat and the himD3::cat alleles were transferred from strain HN1491 and strain K2704 to a JA134 background by P1 transduction, yielding strains JA184 and JA185. Introduction of each of these IHF mutations produced a fourfold decrease in β-galactosidase activity in these mutant strains compared with that of the isogenic wild type (data not shown). These results suggest that IHF activates yiaK-S expression.

<comment datatype="string">The basal level of <i>rsd</i> transcription is maintained by using the downstream rsdp2 promoter recognized by E&sigma;<sup>70</sup>. On the basis of sequence similarity and unique expression patterns, such as the inverse relationship with the growth rate, the rsdp2 promoter can be classified as a member of the gearbox family of promoters, but it cannot be transcribed by E&sigma;<sup>38</sup> <i>in vivo</i> or <i>in vitro</i>. Under certain circumstances, the upstream sequence including the rsdp1 promoter exerts an inhibitory effect on the rsdp2 function, because the deletion of the rsdp1 region results in an increase in transcription from the downstream rsdp2 promoter. The mechanism of inhibition by the upstream sequence remains unsolved.</comment>

<comment datatype="string">~90% of the <i>ptsG</i> mRNA is transcribed from a major promoter, P1 (ptsGp1) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9767573">Plumbridge98a</a>].
<p>
A third promoter in the region located between <i>ptsG</i>p1 and <i>ptsG</i>p2 was identified by <i>in vitro</i> transcription and by RNA polymerase footprinting techniques, as well as <i>in vivo</i> by S1 analysis and fusions with a <i>lacZ</i> reporter gene [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20668389">Pennetier10</a>]. It expresses a transcript antisense to <i>ptsG</i> that has characteristics more like a divergently expressed cryptic unstable transcript (CUT) than a prokaryotic sRNA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20668389">Pennetier10</a>].
<p>
<i>ptsG</i>p1 was validated experimentally in aerobic conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146601">Chung13</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">ArcA is a dual transcriptional regulator for <b>A</b>noxic <b>r</b>edox <b>c</b>ontrol [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2964639">Iuchi88</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8412675">Iuchi93</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7855430">Gunsalus94</a>]. It acts primarily as a negative transcriptional regulator under anaerobic conditions. ArcA represses operons involved in respiratory metabolism, including those that encode products such as the tricarboxylic acid cycle enzymes, enzymes of the glyoxylate shunt, and enzymes of the pathway for fatty acid degradation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2070418">Iuchi91</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7855430">Gunsalus94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1812811">Lin91</a>]. In addition, ArcA acts as a repressor for <i>rpoS</i> transcription [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16291649">Mika05</a>]. ArcA also activates a few operons encoding proteins involved in fermentative metabolism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8071220">Brondsted94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8892825">Lynch96</a>]. It has been identified as global repressor of carbon oxidation pathways [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. Microarray analyses have identified a large number of genes affected by ArcA and have revealed that the Arc system and the FNR regulatory network overlap to a much greater extent than previously estimated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15699038">Salmon05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14711822">Liu04a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15838044">Perrenoud05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. It has been suggested that the most significant role of ArcA is under microaerobic conditions, while that of FNR is under more strictly anaerobic conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12486057">Alexeeva03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15669087">Levanon05</a>]. For full expression of <i>arcA</i> both FNR and ArcA are required [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8022271">Compan94</a>]. Distinct functional roles for both regulators have been proposed, and it has been shown that there is little direct coregulation of the two [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>].
<p>
ArcA is a response regulator and is activated as a DNA-binding protein by phosphorylation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11527965">Jeon01</a>]. The cognate sensor kinase ArcB is membrane associated and has three cytoplasmic domains; a transmitter, a receiver, and a phosphotransfer (HPt) domain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7957084">Ishige94</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1597416">Iuchi92a</a>]. Under anaerobic conditions ArcA is phosphorylated in a phosphorelay reaction that involves phosphotransfer from the autophosphorylated transmitter domain of ArcB to the receiver and Hpt domain of ArcB and finally to the receiver domain of ArcA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10851007">Kwon00c</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8825099">Tsuzuki95</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9286997">Georgellis97</a>]. Autophosphorylation of ArcB is stimulated by effectors such as d-lactate, pyruvate, and acetate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10585483">Georgellis99</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10585483">Georgellis99</a>]. Under aerobic conditions, the autokinase activity of ArcB is inhibited by quinone electron carriers [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11423658">Georgellis01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15326287">Malpica04</a>], and unphosphorylated ArcB promotes the dephosphorylation of ArcA-P by a reverse phosphorelay reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9830034">Georgellis98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15838055">PenaSandoval05</a>]. It has been suggested that ArcA may also be subject to cross-regulation by other, unknown sensor kinases [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16291649">Mika05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12366850">Oshima02</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17213678">Kato07a</a>]. Z nucleotides [ZMP (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide-1-beta-D-ribofuranosyl 5-monophosphate) and/or ZTP (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide-1-beta-D-ribofuranosyl 5-triphosphate)] can act as direct phosphodonors to ArcA <i>in vivo</i>, activating it in an ArcB-independent manner [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33318202">VazquezCiros20</a>].
<p>
ArcA is a member of the OmpR/PhoB subfamily of response regulators and consists of an N-terminal receiver domain and a C-terminal helix-turn-helix DNA-binding domain  [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9205844">Mizuno97</a>]. The crystal structures of the receiver domain of ArcA in the presence and absence of the phosphoryl analog BeF<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> have been solved [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15876365">ToroRoman05a</a>]. In the crystal structures, the receiver domain forms a symmetric dimer.
<p>
ArcA appears to be S-nitrosylated on Cys173 in planktonic cells under aerobic growth conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33850153">Barraud21</a>].
<p>
Weight matrices for the DNA-binding site for ArcA-P have been obtained. The proposed binding site consists of 15 bp with a direct spaced repeat [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15728117">Favorov05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10216875">McGuire99</a>]. It has been suggested that multimerization, induced by phosphorylation, is a prerequisite for binding [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11527965">Jeon01</a>]. ArcA represses transcription by directly binding to the promoter or by binding to sites overlapping an activator-binding site [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16849788">Cho06a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15252051">Jeong04b</a>]. As an activator, it  appears to act as part of a nucleoprotein complex. For activation of <i>pfl</i>, a functional interaction between the ArcA and Fnr protein has been suggested [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1592804">Sawers92</a>]. For expression of <i>cydAB</i>, it has been shown that ArcA-P antagonizes H-NS [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11123679">Govantes00</a>]. At the R1 P<sub>Y</sub> promoter, ArcA acts in conjunction with TraJ. ArcA represses and activates transcription solely by binding DNA, and it activates only indirectly when its binding interferes with the binding and repression of another transcriptional repressor [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. The majority of ArcA-binding sites overlap the &sigma;<sup>70</sup> promoter recognition elements [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>].
<p>
ArcA is not an essential protein [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32108145">Miyake20</a>]. Under glucose-abundant conditions, the double mutant of <i>iclR arcA</i> causes an increase in biomass yield (47%) and reduction of acetate (70%) and CO<sub>2</sub> (16%) production. Under glucose-limited conditions, this double mutant exhibits an increase of biomass of only 13% [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21481254">Waegeman11</a>]. On the other hand, in an <i>arcA</i> mutant, the TCA cycle flux was increased 4.4 times above that of the wild type in the presence of nitrates, and the intracellular ATP/ADP ratio increased approximately 2-fold above that of the wild-type strain [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22790675">Toya12</a>].
<p>
An exhaustive analysis of the ArcA response regulator was carried out, based on different experimental methodologies, High-throughputs (ChIP-chip and ChIP-seq), bioinformatic analysis, DNase I footprinting, and gene expression profiling, and the results showed that ArcA is a global repressor of carbon oxidation pathways [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. ArcA-P directly regulates the expression of 85 operons under anaerobic growth conditions, where 74 operons are repressed and 11 are activated [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. The proportion of phosphorylated ArcA is increased in aerobic conditions and the presence of carbon monoxide (CO) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26907100">Wareham16</a>]. It was shown that most ArcA-binding sites contain additional direct repeat (DR) elements as well as the two required for binding an ArcA dimer, and this finding provided a  novel insight into how ArcA accomplishes global regulation of gene expression [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. More than 50% of the sites have additional DR elements, and the majority of ArcA-binding sites contain three to five DR elements, predominantly at a CTC spacing of 11 bp [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>]. The variations in the number, spacing, location, and predicted strength of DR elements within the chromosomal ArcA-binding regions suggest plasticity in the architecture of ArcA-binding sites for either repressed or activated operons [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24146625">Park13d</a>].
<p>
The growth [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28573283">Kargeti17</a>] and the net final biomass produced in an <i>arcA</i> single-deletion mutants  growing under anaerobic fermentation conditions were affected relative to responses of the wild-type strain (<i>Escherichia coli</i> strain BW25113) grown in the same conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28573283">Kargeti17</a>]. <i>arcA</i> deletion increased expression of genes involved in acetate assimilation and uptake and also genes involved in the TCA cycle [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29193870">Veeravalli18</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. The mutant also caused decreased nucleotide synthesis, decreased glucose and ammonia uptake rates, and enhanced nitrogen transport and accumulation of amino acids and their precursors, as well as derepression of alternate carbon metabolic proteins [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. The activities of some transcription factors appear to be enhanced (ArgR, NtrC, NrdR) in the arcA mutant, whereas others are diminished (PuuR) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33785570">Iyer21</a>]. [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29748694">Kargeti18</a>] et al. reported a relative increase in glucose uptake rate above that required for the observed growth rate in an arcA mutant. In addition, higher ATP synthesis and redox balance rates were reported relative to the observed growth rate and biomass yield in the mutant [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29748694">Kargeti18</a>].
<p>
ArcA promotes dehydration tolerance, both independently and through ArcZ or RpoS [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29457688">Chen18c</a>].
<p>
The accumulation of the protein ArcA is decreased during iron-limiting conditions [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31235512">Zupok19</a>]. A negative correlation between cellular growth and the copy number of the proteins ArcA has been reported [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35694815">Parisutham22</a>].
<p>
ArcA is a flux sensor for the oxygen consumption rate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32383263">Nochino20</a>].
<p>
Under ampicillin treatment, the activity of ArcA appears to increase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/33731833">Deter21</a>].
<p>
Deletion of <i>arcA</i> and <i>gutM</i> under three different antibiotics, cefixime, ciprofloxacin, and chloramphenicol, significantly suppressed resistance evolution, which was not caused by epistatic interactions with mutations known to confer drug resistance [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32144279">Horinouchi20</a>].
<p>
When cells are grown in acetate as a carbon source, the knockout mutants of <i>arcA</i> and <i>fis</i> show an improved growth rate and enhanced acetate uptake [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35416487">Jindal22</a>]. This is a consequence of the reprogramming of the carbon metabolic flux generated by the mutants [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35416487">Jindal22</a>].
<p>
A review of the regulation of molybdenum cofactor (Moco) biosynthesis and molybdoenzyme gene expression via molybdenum and iron by FNR, NarXL/QP, Fur, and ArcA has been published [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31517366">Zupok19a</a>].
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35442087">Brown22</a>]</comment>

observed: To test if l-lyxose itself or an intermediate metabolite was the inducer of the arabinose system, a Tn5 insertion mutant in the rhaA gene (encoding rhamnose isomerase) was obtained from strain JA134 (strain JA199) by using phage λ 467 (b221 cIts857 rex::Tn5 Oam29 Pam80) (4). This mutant was selected by its inability to utilize l-lyxose and the inability to excrete l-rhamnulose when grown in the presence of l-rhamnose. The precise location of the insertion in rhaA was assessed by cloning and sequencing the chromosomal region close to the Tn5 by using an internal sequence of the transposon as a primer. Induction of the ara operon by l-lyxose in strain JA199 indicated that this compound was directly activating the arabinose operon expression.

observed: Expression plasmid pPlaR used for over-expression and purification of His-tagged PlaR was constructed essentially according to the standard procedure9. For construction of plasmid for PlaR expression, a DNA fragment corresponding to the PlaR-coding sequence was amplified by PCR and cloned into pET21a(+) (Novagen) between NdeI and NotI sites, leading to construct pPlaR. For protein expression, pPlaR plasmid was transformed into E. coli BL21 (DE3). Transformants were grown in LB medium and PlaR expression was induced by adding 1 mM IPTG in the middle of exponential growth phase. PlaR protein was purified by the affinity purification procedure with use of a Ni-nitrilotriacetic acid (NTA) agarose column. The affinity-purified PlaR protein was stored frozen in the storage buffer at −80 °C until use. Protein purity was more than 95% as checked by SDS-PAGE.

observed: The gel shift assay was performed as described previously54. The probes of promoter region were synthesized using a set of primers (Table S1a), BW25113 genome as a template, and Ex Taq DNA polymerase (TAKARA). For gel shift assays, 0.5 pmol each of the probes was incubated at 37 °C for 20 min with various amounts of PlaR in 15 ml of gel shift buffer consisting of 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.8 at 4 °C, 150 mM NaCl, and 3 mM Mg acetate. In the case of addition of chemical compounds, 1 ml of various concentrations of chemical compounds was added and incubated for another 20 min. After addition of a DNA dye solution, the mixture was directly subjected to 5% PAGE. The probe DNA in gels was stained by Gel-Red (Biotium) and detected using LAS-4000 IR multi-colour (GE healthcare).

binding.version: Inspected complete primary article body; original PMC6958661.xml retrieved 2026-10-12

observed:
PlaR was shown to repress some of the operons or genes for utilization of plant-derived nutrients. In order to identify a possible inducer ligand(s) for derepression of the yiaK operon (the major regulatory target of PlaR), we first tried to identify metabolites affecting the binding in vitro of PlaR to the yiaK promoter. First we tested 10 mM concentrations of various carbon sources, and found significant reduction of PlaR binding for two metabolites, L-ascorbate and α-D-galacturonate (Fig. 8a). However, D-glucuronate, another degradation product of pectin, did not affect PlaR binding to the yiaK promoter.

Search for inducer candidates for derepression of the yiaK promoter by PlaR. 2.5 uM of Purified PlaR was mixed with 0.5 pM of a DNA probe corresponding to the promoter sequence of yiaK gene. The yiaK promoter formed stable complexes with PlaR as shown in Fig. 3. observed: We then examined the possible influence of the two effective metabolites, L-ascorbate and α-D-galacturonate, on the induction of the yiaK operon. Both the metabolites induced a dose-dependent dissociation in vitro of PlaR from the PlaR-yiaK promoter complex (Fig. 8b). observed: Cultures of strain JA134 carrying φ(yiaK-lacZ) grown in the presence of glucose, both aerobically and anaerobically, showed lower β-galactosidase activities, indicating that glucose produced catabolite repression in this promoter. The addition of cyclic AMP (cAMP) to a 5 mM concentration partially recovered the activity in the presence of glucose. The threefold increased expression of φ(yiaK-lacZ) by growth on succinate (Table 2), which is considered a poor carbon source, also confirmed the regulation of this operon by carbon sources. In contrast, the presence of glucose enhanced the promoter function of the regulator, as indicated by the increased β-galactosidase activity of φ(yiaJ-lacZ). No relevant effect of the cAMP addition was observed in this case. This is further supported by the increase in the expression of (yiaJ-lacZ) fusion (510 Miller units) and the reduction of the expression of (yiaK-lacZ) fusion (55 Miller units) in strain JA186 lacking Crp. Thus, yiaK-S transcription is coordinately repressed in the presence of glucose by both the effect of the absence of cAMP-Crp binding to the promoter and the increase in repressor synthesis.

observed: Among 80 different compounds tested, only l-fucose and l-ascorbate resulted in modestly increased expression of β-galactosidase activity (Table 2). No induction was seen with any of the other compounds, including pentoses, hexoses, other derivative sugars, mono- and dicarboxylate organic acids, and related compounds listed in Materials and Methods. The possibility of the presence of the inducer in animal gut or lung mucus was explored by using rat specimens suspended in minimal medium and autoclaved. These solutions were added to CAA medium at a final concentration of 0.1%. No induction of β-galactosidase activity was detected by growth in any of these cultures.

The inspected abstract describes a dimeric L-xylulose kinase with two 55-kDa subunits and phosphorylation at position 5. Its full original article was not acquired; later 2002 evidence supports additional 3-keto-L-gulonate activity.

binding.version: NCBI PubMed batch original; only exact PMID abstract inspected; full article unavailable

observed: <Abstract><AbstractText>A silent gene encoding a kinase that specifically phosphorylates L-xylulose was activated and rendered constitutive in mutant cells of Escherichia coli. L-Xylulose kinase was purified to homogeneity and found to be a dimer of two subunits of 55 kDa, highly specific for L-xylulose with a Km of 0.8 mM, a Vmax of 33 mumol/min/mg, and an optimum pH of 8.4. Physical (thin layer chromatography) and spectroscopic (nuclear magnetic resonance and optical rotation) characterization of the product of L-xylulose kinase indicated that the enzyme phosphorylated the sugar at position 5. The gene encoding L-xylulose kinase was mapped in the 80.2 min region of the chromosome by conjugation and transduction. Cloning and comparison of the restriction map with the Kohara map (Kohara, Y., Akiyame, K., and Isono, K. (1987) Cell 50, 495-501) located the gene between positions 3963 and 3965 kilobases. The molecular and functional features of L-xylulose kinase together with the location of the corresponding gene indicate that this enzyme did not derive from mutation of any other known kinase. The new kinase opens a route for the utilization of L-lyxose through the action of rhamnose permease, rhamnose isomerase, and the phosphorylation of the L-xylulose formed to L-xylulose 5-phosphate, which is then introduced into the pentose phosphate pathway for subsequent metabolism.</AbstractText></Abstract>

evidence.source_assertion: The inspected abstract links an IS1-mediated 920-kb chromosomal inversion to constitutive yiaK-S expression in the adapted background. The full original article was not acquired.

binding.version: NCBI PubMed batch original; only exact PMID abstract inspected; full article unavailable

observed: <Abstract><AbstractText>The regulator of the yiaK-S operon, currently assigned a carbohydrate utilization function in Escherichia coli, is inactivated by a genome rearrangement that leads to the constitutive expression of the operon. The yiaK-S constitutive cells acquire the ability to utilize the rare pentose L-lyxose. Restriction analysis and sequencing of the regulator gene indicate that it is disrupted by foreign DNA. The insert consists of a large inverted fragment of DNA of 920 kilobases flanked by two IS1 elements with opposite polarity. One corresponds to that found naturally at min 0.4 of the bacterial chromosome and the other to a new copy transposed into the regulator gene located at min 80.6. This insertion-inversion could be the result of the intramolecular transposition mechanism itself, a gene rearrangement rarely originated by IS1. Alternatively, it could be attributed to the homologous recombination between the IS1 at min 0.4 and the IS1 transposed intermolecularly into the yiaK-S regulator gene. The participation of a rare IS1-mediated inversion in the evolution of a stable phenotype is thus identified.</AbstractText></Abstract>

evidence.source_assertion: Northern blots show increased plaR mRNA after deletion of KdgR, supporting a negative influence on plaR expression under these conditions. Regulation may be indirect; direct promoter binding is not established.

binding.version: Inspected complete primary article body; original PMC6958661.xml retrieved 2026-10-12

observed: Since co-regulation was suggested between PlaR and KdgR, we also examined transcription level of the PlaR-target genes in the absence of KdgR by using Northern blot analysis. In the absence of KdgR, transcription increased for the eda, kdgT, kdgK and kduD genes, which were the known targets of KdgR. In addition, the increase of mRNA was also observed for the glpT and glpA gene (Fig. 5, compare lanes 1 and 3), implying the novel targets of KdgR. It is noteworthy that the level of plaR mRNA significantly increased in the absence of KdgR whereas kdgR mRNA increased in the absence of PlaR. This finding suggests a regulatory interplay between the two transcription factors, PlaR and KdgR.

evidence.source_assertion: Figure 5 compares BW25113 with plaR- and kdgR-defective derivatives in M9 plus 0.5% casamino acids, 37 C, aerobic shaking; RNA was sampled at mid-exponential phase for Northern blots.

binding.version: Inspected complete primary article body; original PMC6958661.xml retrieved 2026-10-12

observed: Influence of PlaR on transcription of the regulatory target genes. E. coli wild-type BW25113 (lane 1) and its plaR-defective mutant (lane 2) and kdgR-defective mutant (lane 3) were grown in M9-casamino acids (0.5%) medium at 37 °C with shaking under aerobic conditions. In the middle of exponential phase, total RNA was extracted from each culture and subjected to Northern blot analysis. DIG-labelled hybridization probes are shown on the left side of each panel. The amounts of total RNA analyzed were determined by measuring the intensity of ribosomal RNAs.

evidence.source_assertion: Methods identify BW25113, JW3546 (plaR deletion) and JW1816 (kdgR deletion) for Northern blots. The K-12 protein and MG1655 gene accessions provide reference identities; the reported experiment used these BW25113 derivatives.

binding.version: Inspected complete primary article body; original PMC6958661.xml retrieved 2026-10-12

observed: E. coli DH5α was used for plasmid amplification. E. coli BL21 (DE3) was used for PlaR expression and purification. E. coli K-12 W3110 type-A for genome DNA segments used for gSELEX. E. coli K-12 BW2511352 and its single-gene deletion mutants, JW3546 (plaR) and JW1816 (kdgR)53, were obtained from the E. coli Stock Center (National Bio-Resource Center) for the assays of cell growth, promoter activity and Northern blotting. JW3546 lacking a Km marker was constructed in this study. Cells were grown in LB or M9 minimal media with supplemented 0.2% of galacturonate or 0.5% of Casamino acids at 37 °C under aeration with constant shaking at 150 r.p.m. When necessary, 20 μg ml−1 kanamycin was added into the medium. Cell growth was monitored by measuring the turbidity at 600 nm.

Pectinase-digested citrus or apple pectin increased the yiaJ-lacZ reporter 10-20-fold in ECL1 but not JA134. Structural-gene expression was unaffected even without the repressor; the authors left the significance unresolved.

binding.version: Inspected complete primary article body; original PMC94634.html retrieved 2026-10-12

observed: As described above, citrus fruit pectin or apple pectin previously hydrolyzed by the action of pectinase did not affect the expression of the structural genes, even in the absence of repressor. However, a 10- to 20-fold induction of φ(yiaJ-lacZ) was observed only in wild-type strain ECL1, but not in mutant strain JA134. At present, we do not know the significance of this effect.

evidence.source_assertion: Pectin was prepared at 0.14% in sodium acetate at pH 4.0, digested overnight at 25 C with 400 U of Aspergillus niger pectinase, then diluted tenfold into medium. The tested hydrolysate is an undefined mixture, not an identified PlaR ligand.

binding.version: Inspected complete primary article body; original PMC94634.html retrieved 2026-10-12

observed: Cells were grown on Luria broth or minimal medium and harvested at the end of the exponential phase as described previously (4). Carbon sources were added to a basal inorganic medium at a 60 mM carbon concentration for aerobic growth and 120 mM for anaerobic growth. For anaerobic respiration, nitrate was also added to the culture at a 20 mM concentration. Casein acid hydrolysate (CAA) was used at 0.5 or 1% depending on oxygen availability. To search for the inducer, a screening of candidate molecules was set up by adding to the CAA medium the following compounds at the carbon concentration indicated above: d-raffinose (C18); d-glucopyranosyl-d-fructose, cellobiose, saccharose, trehalose, and maltose (C12); N-acetylmuramic acid (C11); N-acetylglucosamine (C8); methyl-d-mannopyranoside, pimelic acid, and d-glucoheptonic acid (C7); d-galactose, d-fucose, l-fucose, d-fructose, l-fructose, d-mannose, l-mannose, d-sorbose, l-sorbose, inulin, d-glucose, d-tagatose, d-allose, d-talose, d-psicose, l-rhamnose, d-mannitol, d-sorbitol, myo-inositol, dulcitol, l-fucitol, l-iditol, gluconic acid, galacturonic acid, glucuronic acid, saccharic acid, phthalic acid, l-ascorbic acid, and adipic acid (C6); d-arabinose, l-arabinose, d-xylose, l-xylose, d-lyxose, l-lyxose, d-arabitol, l-arabitol, d-ribose, d-ribulose, d-xylulose, adonitol, xylitol, α-ketoglutaric acid, β-ketoglutaric acid (C5); erythritol, succinic semialdehyde, succinic acid, fumaric acid, d,l-malic acid, tartaric acid, diglycolic acid (C4); d-lactate, l-lactate, d,l-glyceraldehyde, glycerol, pyruvic acid (C3); and glycolic acid and oxalic acid (C2). Citrus fruit pectin and apple pectin were prepared at 0.14% in sodium acetate buffer (pH 4.0) and incubated overnight at 25°C with 400 U of Aspergillus niger pectinase, and the hydrolysis products were diluted 10-fold in the medium. All compounds tested were obtained from Sigma Chemical Co. (St. Louis, Mo.).
